title: How to prepare for customer escalation calls on Mac: a routine for product managers
metaTitle: Prepare for Customer Escalation Calls on Mac: PM Routine
description: Prepare for customer escalation calls with one brief, one timeline and one owner. Fixes product managers can use on a Mac today, with or without Lazur.
secondaryKeywords: how to run a customer escalation call
intro: To prepare for customer escalation calls, gather the facts, write a one-page brief, and agree on one owner before anyone joins. Escalation calls go wrong when the product manager hears the whole problem for the first time while the customer is listening. This guide gives you a routine you can run on a Mac with tools you already use: Notion, Slack, Linear, Calendar, and Notes.
tldr: Write the brief before the call, not during it. One page is enough.
Pull links to the facts into one place: the thread, the ticket, the account.
Open with the outcome you need, then name one owner and one next step.
Send a written recap within the hour, while the details are still fresh.
Lazur can draft the brief and take dictated notes, but you own the facts and the promise.

blocks.text: An escalation call usually follows a problem that already failed somewhere else. Support could not fix it, an account owner is worried, or a bug has sat in triage too long. You get pulled in because your role suggests you can make a decision. That is why these calls feel rushed, even when someone put them on your calendar.
Why escalation calls catch you unprepared

Escalation calls rarely arrive with a clear agenda. Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index found that 57% of meetings are ad hoc calls without a calendar invite. About one in ten scheduled meetings is booked at the last minute. Escalations sit in that unplanned group. You get a Slack message that says 'can you hop on with the customer?' and that is the whole briefing.

Treat these numbers as context, not as measurements of escalation calls. I did not find a study or survey that counts how often escalation calls go unprepared, or what they cost. The figures show how often unplanned calls happen and how scattered the work day feels. That is the setting where prep usually gets skipped.
The three questions to answer before you dial in

Before any escalation call, you should answer three questions in one sentence each. If you cannot answer one, that becomes your first task. Write the answers at the top of a note, so you can read them in the first minute of the call.

items: What happened, in the customer's words and in ours.
What the customer needs from this call, such as a fix date, a workaround, or a decision to stay.
What we can commit to today, and who owns each commitment.

blocks.text: The answers should be short. If your first answer runs to three paragraphs, you have not understood the problem yet. Ask the account owner or support lead one question, then rewrite the answer. A clear sentence is easier to say out loud than a long story.
Build a one-page brief in Notion

A brief is one page with five parts: the account, the timeline, the current state, the open questions, and the next step. Keep it under a page. If it runs longer, nobody reads it while the customer is talking. The table below shows what goes in each section, with an example from a typical enterprise escalation.

rows: Customer name, plan, renewal date, account owner
Enterprise plan, renewal this quarter, owner is the account executive
Dated events from first report to today
Ticket opened, bug reproduced, fix planned, fix slipped to next sprint
What is true right now, in one sentence
Exports fail for large files. A manual workaround exists.
Facts you do not know yet
Does this customer run exports every night?
One action with an owner and a date
Engineering names an owner for the fix before end of day
blocks.caption: A brief template you can copy into a Notion page

blocks.text: In Notion, create a new page called Escalation brief and paste the table. Give each section its own heading, so you can scan it fast during the call. If you want a contents list at the top, see [how to add table of contents in Notion](/how-to/add-a-table-of-contents-in-notion).
Reuse the same page for every escalation. The first brief takes the longest. By the fourth or fifth escalation, you will copy the page and fill in the blanks.
Gather facts without a scavenger hunt

Most facts already exist. They sit in a Slack thread, a Linear issue, a support ticket, and an email from the account owner. Your job is to pull links into one place before the call. You do not need to reread everything.

On a Mac, press ⌘K in Slack to open the quick switcher. Type the customer's channel name and open the latest thread. In Linear, press ⌘K to open the command menu, then search for the issue ID. Copy each link into the timeline section of your brief.

Use links, not summaries. A link lets you check the source in one click during the call. A summary can be wrong, and you will not have time to argue with it. Put the link next to the fact it supports.
Write an agenda built around one outcome

An escalation call needs an outcome, not a tour of the problem. Write the outcome as the first line of the agenda. For example: 'Agree on a workaround the customer accepts, and a fix date that engineering has confirmed.' The rest of the agenda supports that line.

Share the agenda in the calendar invite or in the customer's Slack channel, if the customer agrees. HBR argues that meeting outcomes depend on preparation. Its article says new managers are rarely taught how to run a strong meeting. It cites no study for that claim, so treat it as advice, not proof.

blocks.title: Keep internal notes internal
blocks.text: Do not share risk ratings, internal blame, or names of people who are not in the room. The agenda goes to the customer. The brief stays with your team.
Run the call with one owner and one next step

Name a note taker before you join. It can be you, but a second person frees you to listen. Say the one decision you need from the customer. Near the end, state the next step out loud, with the owner and the date. Repeat it, so the customer hears the same commitment you heard.
Worked example: a broken export before a renewal

Say a customer's CSV export fails for large files. Support has an open ticket. The account owner asks you to join a call because the renewal is close. The call slot is short. You have a brief to fill in before you dial.

Before the call, you open the brief. The account section shows an enterprise plan with a renewal this quarter. The timeline has three dated events from support. The Linear issue is in triage with no owner. Your open question is whether this customer runs exports every night, because that decides how urgent the fix is.

On the call, you lead with the outcome. You say the bug is in triage with no owner, and that you will not promise a fix date until engineering names one. You offer a manual workaround. The customer agrees to a check-in. You name the next step: engineering assigns an owner before the end of the day. You post the recap before you hang up.
Mistakes people make on escalation calls

items: Explaining the whole history. The customer knows their pain. Lead with the current state.
Promising a date before engineering confirms it. A soft date becomes a hard date in the customer's notes.
Asking the customer for facts that support already has. Check the ticket first.
Ending the call without a named owner. Everyone assumes someone else will follow up.
Sending the recap the next day. Details blur, and the customer fills the gap with their own version.
Joining alone with no notes. One person listens, the other records decisions.

blocks.text: Edge cases to plan for

Some calls are about trust, not a bug. The customer may ask for a senior person. If so, say who will join and what that person can decide. Do not bring in a senior leader as a stand-in for a decision nobody has made.

Internal escalations need the same brief. A sales leader may escalate a deal, or a support lead may escalate a churn risk. Ask for the deal stage and the decision maker before you join. If the request is about a feature, check the roadmap in Notion before you promise anything.

blocks.title: Check the data rules first
blocks.text: If the customer works in health, finance, or another regulated field, follow your employer's rules on client or patient data. Check them before you paste account details into a brief or an AI tool.
After the call: the recap that closes the loop

Send the recap within the hour, while the details are fresh. Write three lines: what was decided, what each owner will do, and when the customer hears next. Post it in the customer's Slack channel, and link the Linear issue so engineering sees the same facts.
Lazur can help with the recap. Hold fn and dictate your notes at the cursor in Notion or Slack. Then ask Lazur to draft the recap text. You still check each fact against the links before you send it.
Where Mac tools help and where they stop

Apple's Calendar User Guide covers adding events and managing notifications. Apple's Notes User Guide covers creating notes and sharing them. Neither guide describes a meeting-prep workflow or links notes to events. So you attach the brief link yourself. In Calendar, choose File > New Event or press ⌘N, then paste the link into the event details.
Third-party note and calendar apps promise prep features. I did not test them for this page, so this guide sticks to the apps you probably already have.
Keep the routine small enough to repeat

Do not build a new system before your next call. Use one Notion page, one Slack link, and one Linear link. Reuse the same brief, so each escalation starts faster than the last. After a few calls, you will see which section you skip. Cut that section, and keep the rest.

faq.question: How long should I spend preparing for a customer escalation call?
faq.answer: Spend less time on slides and more time on facts. If you can answer the three questions in one sentence each, you are ready. If you cannot, the gap tells you what to check before you join.

faq.question: What if I do not have enough facts to prepare?
faq.answer: Say so, and say when you will have them. Tell the customer what you know, what you are checking, and when you will come back. A clear gap is better than a confident guess.

faq.question: Should I send the agenda to the customer?
faq.answer: Usually yes, if it helps them and the customer agrees. Keep it short and put the outcome first. Leave out internal notes, risk ratings, and names of people who are not on the call.

faq.question: Can Lazur join the call or speak for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not join calls or operate other apps for you. You can hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. You still speak and make the decision.

faq.question: Is an escalation brief the same as a PRD?
faq.answer: No. A PRD describes what to build. A brief describes one problem, one account, and one next step. Keep them separate, so the brief does not grow into a spec.

faq.question: What if the customer asks for a fix date on the call?
faq.answer: Ask who owns the work and what engineering has confirmed. If nobody has confirmed a date, offer the day you will know, and name who will tell the customer.

faq.question: Does this routine need a Mac app?
faq.answer: No. The routine uses Notion, Slack, and Linear, which you can run in a browser or in their desktop apps. Lazur itself runs on macOS on Apple silicon and Intel. Windows is planned, not available.

costs.title: Customer trust
costs.text: The customer hears 'let me check' a second time and starts to doubt the team. Trust is easier to protect in the first call than to rebuild after a third. Each vague answer adds to the doubt.

costs.title: Commitments you cannot keep
costs.text: A date said on a call becomes a date the customer holds you to. If engineering later misses it, you own the miss, even though you never owned the work. The cost lands on your name.

costs.title: Engineering time
costs.text: A vague follow-up pulls two engineers into a long thread. One clear message with a named owner would have answered the question in a few minutes. The extra back and forth is the hidden cost.

costs.title: Focus and interruptions
costs.text: Microsoft's telemetry says employees are interrupted every 2 minutes by a meeting, email, or notification. An unplanned escalation call lands in that same stream. It breaks the planning work you meant to do that afternoon.

costs.title: A second call
costs.text: A call that ends without an owner tends to produce another call. You pay the cost twice, once in the meeting and again in the follow-up. The second call is usually shorter and less friendly.

causes.title: Escalations arrive unscheduled
causes.text: Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index found that 57% of meetings are ad hoc calls without a calendar invite. Escalations usually fall into that unplanned group. You get little warning, so there is little time to prepare.

causes.title: Context lives in too many places
causes.text: Microsoft reports that 48% of employees say their work feels chaotic and fragmented. When the facts sit in four tools, the prep step is the first thing that gets skipped. You run out of time before you find the thread.

causes.title: Nobody teaches the prep step
causes.text: HBR argues that meeting success tracks preparation, and that new managers are rarely taught how to run a strong meeting. The article cites no study, so read it as expert opinion about a gap that is easy to miss.

causes.title: Meeting culture rewards talk
causes.text: Atlassian's State of Teams 2024 says that in organizations with poor meeting cultures, people spend 50% more time in unnecessary meetings. The page does not name a source for that figure, so treat it as a directional signal.

causes.title: Ownership is unclear
causes.text: When a bug has no owner, nobody can answer the customer's question. The product manager ends up holding the question, the escalation, and the apology at the same time. That load makes prep feel impossible.

causes.title: Preparation gets interrupted
causes.text: Notifications and messages break up focus. If Slack is open all morning, the brief never gets written. For a fix, see [how to stop Slack interruptions on Mac](/for/product-managers/problems/slack-interruptions-break-focus-pm).

fixes.title: Write one brief for every escalation
fixes.text: Use the five-part brief from this guide. Keep it on one page. Reuse the same Notion page, so you do not start from a blank screen each time. The template gets faster with every call.

fixes.title: Collect links, not summaries
fixes.text: Put a link next to each fact. In Slack, press ⌘K to find the thread fast. In Linear, press ⌘K to find the issue. A link lets you verify a fact during the call, which a summary cannot do.

fixes.title: State the outcome before the agenda
fixes.text: Write one sentence that says what a good call looks like. If you cannot write it, you are not ready to join. Put that sentence first in the invite and in your own notes.

fixes.title: Name one owner and one next step
fixes.text: Before the call ends, say who does what and by when. Ask the customer to repeat it back. A named owner turns a conversation into work that someone can track.

fixes.title: Send the recap within the hour
fixes.text: Use three lines: the decision, the owner, and the next contact. Post the recap where the customer already talks, and link the Linear issue for the engineering team. Short recaps get read.

fixes.title: Dictate notes, then draft
fixes.text: Hold fn and dictate your call notes at the cursor. Ask Lazur to draft the recap, then check every fact yourself. Lazur drafts text. It does not decide what you promise.

fixes.title: Protect focus before and after
fixes.text: Put a short focus block in Calendar before the call and after it. Mute Slack during that time. The brief is easier to write when you are not switching tasks every few minutes.

fixes.title: Refuse dates with no owner
fixes.text: Set a rule for yourself: no fix date goes to a customer until engineering names an owner. Offer the day of the next update instead. That answer is easier to keep than a guess.

plan.label: Day 1
plan.title: Gather the facts
plan.text: Open the customer's Slack channel and the Linear issue. Copy the links into one Notion page. Write down what you do not know yet, one line per gap.

plan.label: Day 2
plan.title: Write the brief template
plan.text: Create one Notion page with five sections: account, timeline, current state, open questions, and next step. Reuse it for every escalation so you never start from a blank page.

plan.label: Day 3
plan.title: Write the outcome line
plan.text: Write the outcome sentence for your next likely call. Read it aloud. Cut any part of the agenda that does not support that sentence.

plan.label: Before the call
plan.title: Read the brief once
plan.text: Read the brief once, slowly, and answer the three questions. Mark any answer you cannot give as a gap to close before you join.

plan.label: During the call
plan.title: Name the owner
plan.text: Say the owner and the next step out loud. Assign one person to take notes, and ask the customer to repeat the commitment back to you.

plan.label: After the call
plan.title: Send the recap
plan.text: Post the three-line recap in the customer's Slack channel within the hour. Link the Linear issue and update the brief with what changed.

plan.label: Day 5
plan.title: Review the template
plan.text: Check which sections you skipped during the week. Remove the ones that did not change the call, and keep the ones that did.
